utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Odalovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In a moment your examination by Mr. Fila will continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the outset of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did the events in Kosovo and Metohija attract attention from the international community and representatives of the international community?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the events in Kosovo and Metohija in 1997 and 1998 did attract a great deal of attention of international representatives and of international public opinion so that in that period numerous teams of journalists and diplomatic representatives, both those who were already in the country and others who came ad hoc, came to visit Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you or the district which you headed had a service or special personnel for foreign policy activities?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the duties of the district and my own duties, those activities were not envisaged but the situation required that as head of the district, or rather, deputy head and then head, I had a large number of contacts with international representatives. We didn't have appropriate services to keep track of all these activities so that this was quite a problem for me, which took a lot of time and attention away from my regular duties so that in the period from 1997/1998 I received several hundred foreign journalists and diplomats.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you didn't have any such specialised service, did you take any steps to respond to the needs that arose in this period?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my regular reports that I sent to the governments of the Republic of Serbia, I briefed them about my activities but I also drew attention to the fact that developments were such that required greater support. I simply was not able to do all that myself. I even addressed myself to Mr. Zivadin Jovanovic, who was minister of foreign affairs at the time, because diplomats of higher and higher rank were coming to Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you receive any such support for assistance from the republic's government?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first form of support that I received from the government of the republic was the appointment of Ante Milosavljevic as a coordinator of the state bodies for the area of Kosovo and Metohija and shortly after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did the federal government respond?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal government did respond. First the Ministry of Foreign Affairs opened an office, to which it sent several staff members from the foreign ministry to assist me and Mr. Milosavljevic, who was confronted with the same problems as I was so that this office was of great benefit for our activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did anyone else join you later on to assist in foreign affairs activities?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this office was opened in the summer of 1998 Mr. Nikola Sainovic arrived in Pristina, which I considered to be of great support and assistance because he was, after all, vice-president of the federal government who was able with full authority to talk to foreign diplomats and provide much better answers than I was able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Had you known Mr. Sainovic from before?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Mr. Sainovic because for a certain time he was prime minister of the Republic of Serbia at the time when the districts were being formed so that I did have contact with him at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was his position when he arrived?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time he was vice-president of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when he came to Kosovo, which duties did he take over?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be as precise as possible. He helped me most. He took over these contacts with foreign diplomats, which was of greatest assistance to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And did Sainovic take over the duties that you had carried out? I'm not referring to these contacts but other duties.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not any of the duties which were part of my regular responsibilities except for what I have said. So I continued with my work unhindered for which I had far more time and ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did you cooperate with Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our cooperation took the form of brief meetings, consultations, discussions regarding certain problems. Some foreign journalists and diplomats of lower rank by inertia continued to coming to see me, but we channelled them over gradually. But still I had to ask Mr. Sainovic for his advice and we had to exchange opinions about these visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When was this cooperation between you and Sainovic developing?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Main Board of the SBS sent certain officials to Kosovo and Metohija in July 1998?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be quite frank. I was very glad to see that another three very prominent officials came to Kosovo: Mr. Minic, Mr. Andjelkovic, and Mr. Markovic. I don't know who sent them, whether it was the Main Board of the SBS, of which I was not a member; but in any event I felt that their presence there could facilitate the situation for the simple reason that attacks by terrorist bands and the overall situation was most disturbing for the Serbian population and other non-Albanians. We were under a great deal of pressure from the population and threats to evacuate so that the situation was extremely tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What kind of activities did they engage in?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was able to see through contacts with them and on the ground, their main concern was political activities. Mr. Matkovic was also a businessman, so he was general manager of Sartid and he had two factories in Kosovo and Metohija. Mr. Andjelkovic was mostly in the field contacting the people directly, and Mr. Andjelkovic was perhaps the most experienced in political matters, so he monitored political developments. And it was in that context that I had contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you aware whether these officials of the SBS participated in meetings in the building of the Executive Council in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, there were certain activities in the civilian sector with these three officials or with each of them individually I would meet quite often because the situation as of June, especially in the Pristina and the surroundings, these contacts with civilian bodies were extremely necessary. This was also a period of time when we had formed headquarters for supplies. The population was in a panic and they were at risk, which made such contacts necessary. I remember a specific situation when the mines in Belacevac were taken over by Albanian terrorists, that several villages inhabited by Serbs who were frightened, and they sent a petition for collective evacuation. So I advised those people to talk to these officials directly, whereas I continued with my own activities in the Kosovo district to the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Throughout your stay in Kosovo in 1998, had you heard of the existence of a Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1998 and 1999 I had not heard of the existence of a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you look at tab 6 now, please, Defence Exhibit 2D382. What is this document? Don't read it for us, please, just comment on it briefly.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document on one of the discussions that Mr. Milosavljevic and I had with a certain number of international diplomats. This is with Mr. Miles with whom I had at least 20 meetings and with Mrs. Juliana and we are discussing -- Ms. Julia Taft we are discussing the organisation of humanitarian centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did the American delegation react to your statement and that of Mr. Milosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They responded positively. What they told us was that this was the way in which we should continue to work and the best way to assist the population, because in discussions with them and all other international representatives we made a clear distinction between the Albanian terrorist bands and the Albanian population. We were discussing aid to the entire population which was at risk, and it wasn't only the Serbs and non-Albanians but also the Albanian national minority. And through our humanitarian activities and assistance, no distinction was being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you now look at tab 7, Defence Exhibit 2D72, and will you tell us briefly what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a late-night meeting with Mr. Byrnes and their demand was -- his claim was that in the fero-nickel factory there were 1.000 Albanians being detained. And as this was a late-night meeting when there is a certain procedure required, I promised that I would, as soon as, possible enable a visit and organise a visit to this factory. What I was particularly concerned by was that representatives of this mission went directly to the factory. When they told me about the problem, I enabled their entry into the factory early in the morning the next day, and I was unpleasantly surprised that even though they saw that the report they had received was absolutely not correct, they continued behaving irresponsibly and in spite of everything they saw not a single detained person did they find there nor were any Albanians ever detained there, yet their report was unfavourable. And I told Mr. Shaun Byrnes later on that this was not in a spirit of cooperation and that this was not helpful for anyone, on the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was this an example of the media picture that was being formed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the best example that the truth did not want to be shown because the media reported at length that there were 1.000 detainees; however, when it was proven that there was no one there, not a single person could be hidden, never mind a thousand, so it would have been fair to report that not a single Albanian was detained there. But this was not reported, it was ignored.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Turn to tab 8, 2D103. Look at the document, please, and especially paragraph 5 of this document. Would you please explain it to us.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the lengthier talks I had with Mr. Sesa, the Italian ambassador at the time. Paragraph 5 refers to a very dangerous point in time when there was reaction after the kidnapping of two Serb civilians. As a encounter-measure a group of Albanians were detained and I drew the attention of Mr. Sesa to the danger and possible consequences of such behaviour I said that the state bodies and all of us who were acting on behalf of the state were against any kind of revengism, but I did ask him to use his authority and to start talking to the terrorists in a more serious manner, so that they cease with the kidnappings, that the civilians be released, because we also had incidents of kidnappings. I think we talked about that on the first day. And most of those people never returned to their homes. Our message was, we didn't wish to allow any revenge activities and we asked him to use his influence to put an end to these kidnappings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is this document, Mr. Odalovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document we are looking at, it is a note on my discussion with Mr. Sesa, an official report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who made the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The report was compiled by representatives of this foreign ministry office outpost in Pristina. Mr. Skoric was present on their behalf at this discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Odalovic said something twice regarding the opposition of the state to self-organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So would you repeat that a third time, as it hasn't been reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this occasion, too, talking to Mr. Sesa, as on previous occasions, I appealed to him. First of all, I conveyed the position of the state, that we were against the self-organisation by the population. There was a danger of the Serbs self-organising themselves and responding to kidnappings and abductions of Serbs. So we asked the state bodies to work in that direction and prevent any kind of self-organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you look at paragraph 6, last sentence, please, who is being mentioned there and what is it about?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discussion here was about the kidnappings of two Serb journalists two months prior to this Djuro Slavuj and Ratko Perinic, two journalists who were on assignment and they were never found to this day. I appealed to Mr. Sesa and all foreign diplomats - I don't know who I didn't appeal to - to appeal to the KLA to release the journalists. Unfortunately, we don't know what happened to them to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you look at the next Defence Exhibit 2D120, tab 9. Look at the middle of paragraph 2 and tell us what this documented is, tab 9. When was the meeting held, who attended the meeting, and what was it about?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a meeting with the delegation of the European Commission held on the 18th of November, 1998. Mr. Sartori was there in charge of the renewal programme, then also for the EKO programme, Mr. Levertovski we discussed humanitarian problems and the need for joint efforts for them to join in, that is, the international community, to assist in dealing with an extremely difficult humanitarian situation. Among other things, we discussed the programme of education, the question of supplies for the population, the reconstruction of buildings. They said that they were ready to provide certain assistance. It says here 10 million ECUs for the education programme and 7 million for the accommodation of temporarily displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Odalovic. Mr. Fila, your question was not heard because it overran the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why were you attending that meeting, Mr. Odalovic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two reasons for this. One was that I was in charge of one of the humanitarian headquarters for humanitarian aid for the population in Kosovo district. I was member of the central headquarters formed by the government in 1998. And the second reason was that I was directly involved in the implementation of the agreement signed between Milosevic and Rugova regarding education. This was the implementation stage of that agreement when concrete measures started to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did -- was medical aid mentioned and the touring of certain facilities at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I took advantage of the opportunity when talking to these high-level representatives who were ready to extend humanitarian aid to draw attention to a very difficult problems that our health centre in Pristina was encountering and I appealed to them to visit it. And I felt that they could provide some assistance. The reason for this was that at the clinical centre in Pristina provided medical care to the entire population and at least 90 per cent of the patients were Albanians. There were also Serbs. The medical staff were mixed ethnically so that aid extended would be of the greatest assistance to everyone and they agreed, and as far as I know, they did tour this medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since you were an official of the government in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998, did you know anything about how control was exercised over the Army of Yugoslavia on the one hand and the MUP on the other?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my knowledge goes, what I knew was that both the VJ and the MUP functioned in terms of their respective chains of command. These were evolved, structures evolved bodies. They had their own ways of functions, their own laws and rules. All civilians tried to steer clear of interfere in their business since this happens to be a highly specialised field. Whenever we meddled we would normally get it wrong simply because we could not find our way around. The way they functioned had to do with their rules of subordination and their other rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know what Nikola Sainovic's responsibilities were after the arrival of the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following the Milosevic-Holbrooke and the Jovanovic-Geremek Agreement, the federal government reacted by setting up a special commission in charge of working together with the verification mission. As for our republican level, we were given the task of meeting the verifiers and everybody else who was arriving and to try to get them put up and give them some assistance, but it was noteworthy that a special team was set up to cooperate with them, that was charged with cooperating with these people specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what was Sainovic's role in all of that? What did he do specifically?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of that commission. The commission comprised 13 or 15 members but don't hold me to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was your attitude towards the mission, your private attitude and your professional attitude as well?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's important to point out a fact that I think will answer your question. Everything that the Government of the Republic of Serbia and its official bodies undertook by way of responsibility at the upper-most level would trickle down to us who were district heads. We were instructed to treat this mission and any other mission that might arrive in Kosovo in the spirit of cooperation and in the spirit of any agreements signed by the state. Whoever signed the agreement normally had nothing to do with the implementation stage. It was us functionaries and officials at the lower-most level who normally had to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So who did you report to about all the activities that you were in charge of?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported about all my activities to the Government of the Republic of Serbia. This was a responsibility that I had. I did this on a periodical basis and every six months as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about foreign journalists and all sorts of visiting foreigners, visit and tour Kosovo and Metohija in 1998, in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes there were many foreign journalist crews from the most powerful media stationed in Kosovo. When anti-terrorist activities were stepped-up there was this one specific instance. This was a large-scale delegation of foreign journalists and diplomats sometime in mid-August touring the whole of Kosovo and Metohija. I think it was the 16th of August. I welcomed their plane at the airport. We used two buses and we were underway to tour Kosovo and Metohija. Something that is quite noteworthy is we couldn't take the regular route, the Pristina-Pec road; we had to travel through Montenegro. We had to take the round-about road simply because the usual one wasn't safe. We took the Pec-Decani road and drove through Junik, Prizren, and Dura and we returned to the airport that same evening and the foreign journalists who arrived by plane and left those who were in the Grand Hotel just stayed there and kept on sending out their reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see Sainovic in Pristina during the air-strikes, the NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic came several times during the intense talks with Mr. Rugova, and as the agreement was being drafted, the draft that was later adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you look at tab 11 now, please. This is Exhibit 2356 -- 2365. What is this about, sir? 2D365.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a joint communique, a joint declaration by Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Rugova on the 5th of April. There was a meeting and there were just two salient points that were the result of that meeting: Their agreement and their commitment to a political process as well as their commitment that everybody should do whatever was within their power to bring the displaced persons back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did the most severe air-strikes against civilian targets occur?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day after the agreement was signed, regrettably, between the 6th and the 7th of April. In the evening hours the centre of Pristina was targeted, the post office building was hit, the health and pension central fund building was hit, and as a consequence of this destruction even as we speak the retired persons of Kosovo and Metohija still can't obtain this sort of information because the files were destroyed. The bank building was destroyed as well and the Kosovo district building was destroyed because it was right next to the bank. The Orthodox cemetery in Pristina was targeted [as interpreted] as well. I took a group of foreign journalists over the next day to see what had occurred. There were craters. There were caskets and graves lying open destroyed, but none of these images were ever eventually transmitted for the world to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did the negotiations or the talks with Mr. Rugova end?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It ended towards the end of the month, and the agreement was signed by Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Rugova. I personally attended the signing ceremony. I was glad that the agreement was now signed, and I was hoping that the situation would now begin to change, quite simply that all those operation would come to an end. I was, though, hoping in vain it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you look at tab 12 now, Defence Exhibit 2D375. What is this about, sir?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are decisions by the Temporary Executive Council, one of them being to set up a humanitarian staff to help displaced persons returning to their homes. I am a member of that staff along with Mr. Andric, and representatives of ethnic communities, Albanians, Roma, Turks. This is what the staff was supposed to do. This was our remit in a manner of speaking. We were supposed to provide supplies, foodstuffs, health services, that sort of thing. And this was on the 19th of April, 1998 [as interpreted], during the NATO air-strikes when -- when the population was moving a lot about Kosovo and Metohija. There is another decision here --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was this decision in reference to all ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. If you look at the composition of the staff itself, it's quite obvious. For us the humanitarian aspect was always the upper-most aspect of this situation, and no discrimination was involved, no distinctions were drawn between the various ethnic groups. We provided to all alike to the extent we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This was the 19th, 1999?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1999, during the NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, my last question. We talked about what you do today who you work with and so on and so forth. Did you obtain any figures as to the number of missing persons in Kosovo on both sides? Is there a figure that has been agreed by you on the one hand and the Kosovar side on the other?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most serious consequence of the NATO air-strikes in addition to the victims and the destruction is the number of missing persons, 2.087, that seems to be the figure bandied about by joint lists and this is a figure that has been agreed with the Pristina delegation and the International Committee of the Red Cross. This is one of the least contentious issues to all practical intents. The exact figure concerning the missing persons. About 1.500 Kosovar Albanians and about 580 [as interpreted] Serbs and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the total figure in relation to the victims, the total number of victims?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has not been ascertained with any great degree of certainty. We have this municipal committee for those murdered and kidnapped and the number we obtained was a total of 9.000 roughly speaking. There may be small adjustments to this figure to come, but we used all the information available to us at the time and this is a ball-park figure but it seems to be the most reliable figure available to us up until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what was the break-down for this total?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not our intention to represent this break-down along ethnic lines; it was, however, necessary to our deepest regret. The total would be over 9.000, 2.500 of these were Serbs and other non-Albanians, the remaining part being ethnic Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This brings my examination-in-chief to an end. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, where -- is there any document relating to an agreement with the International Committee of the Red Cross about the number of missing persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first thing that the joint group did, the rules were signed by the Pristina and Belgrade delegations and International Committee of the Red Cross. The list of missing persons was published, it's an official list, and it's in the database of the International Red Cross, the working group was chaired by Mr. Francois from the International Red Cross. This list is public in nature and it's available to anyone who might seek to consult it. I don't have a copy but should the Chamber want me to, I should be able to deliver a copy to the Chamber in no time at all. The order is alphabetical. No discrimination is made along ethnic lines. All those who were victims were treated by us in the same way in terms of method. This is a humanitarian issue and that was the approach that we decided to take as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila, did you refer to tab 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but not 10 because it was used with the previous witness. Tab 3 and tab 4 were mentioned together. There was a single question about these two tabs -- rather, 10 -- Your Honours, it's in order to prevent us tendering the same document five times through different witnesses. Andreja Milosavljevic was already asked about this, this was no need to raise it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Other Defence counsel with questions for this witness? Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but before I start with cross-examination, if you allow me, there is one -- it has to be one correction in transcript, page 15, line 3. I think that witness said: "Representatives of other ethnic communities, Albanians, Roma, and Turks," I think that we miss Albanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyone else cast any light on that? I think we'll have the interpreters check that later and confirm the position, but thank you for drawing it to our attention, Mr. Cepic. Please continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Odalovic, good morning. My name is Djuro Cepic. I'm here on behalf of General Lazarevic, and I'll ask you a number of questions. On Friday during your in chief by my learned friend Fila you mentioned that you were at the head of the civilian protection for the Kosovo district. What I want to know is this: Did the civilian protection unit have anything to do with the VJ in terms of subordination?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had no direct links. We were with the republican civilian protection staff and we had nothing to do with the army or the police. At the time there was certainly no subordination or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Defence Exhibit 5D1239.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Before I ask the question, I'm afraid we have a technical problem. We didn't see the first 20 seconds of this video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours, I would like us to go back to the very beginning of this footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, are you familiar with these images?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about this a while ago. On the 16th of August I met at the Slatina airport. This group of journalists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, you've answered the question counsel put. He will now ask you a specific question I think about your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, you were at Junik on the 16th of August, 1998. We have heard evidence by Colonel Crosland before this Trial Chamber, who was part of the KDOM, indicating that Junik and the surroundings in the spring of 1998 had been razed to the ground. He said this specifically in Exhibit P2645, paragraph 12. He repeats this on page 9920 of the transcript. My question: Is this statement made by Colonel Crosland true?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the case actually was in the spring of 1998, but on this particular day when we were there together, there was obvious damage, yes, both in Prilep, which is near Decani. Prilep had sustained more damage than Junik itself. There was a certain extent of damage in Junik as well and the cameras clearly show that, but razed to the ground would be an overstatement. Life went on even after we left. We'd been to their homes and we saw for ourselves. There was a group comprising 120 foreign journalists and diplomats and they all saw for themselves what the situation was. Over in Prilep, it was quite obvious that the clashes that had occurred there had been more severe and some of the houses had been destroyed to a greater extent than in Junik, but there is something that one should bear in mind. About 20 days before our visit to Junik there had been three incidents, during which three policemen were killed, two in one and one in one of the other two. But just before our arrival policemen had been killed in this village. Therefore, there had certainly been clashes, a certain amount of destruction had been caused, but one certainly can't speak of the village being razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Odalovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please -- [In English] Unfortunately, Your Honour, if you allow me to say, my intention is to play another video-clip but we have technical problems right now so it is not possible from this computer to start that video-clip. So we need assistance as soon as possible please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In which case may I interpose here to say that the citation of the reference of Colonel Crosland's testimony was not entirely accurate, and I don't mean to pass words, but if one looks at his testimony at the page number referred to and his testimony in his statement he says that the town of Junik was razed and I think there is a distinction between saying that these towns in the area were razed and saying that they were razed to the ground, which is what my friend put to the witness twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that is a matter for comment and resolution in due course. It may be the subject of re-examination; that's a matter for you. What do you mean you need assistance, Mr. Cepic? I've no -- are you looking for a technician from --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. In the meantime, if you allow me to say, in relation to the words of my learned friend Mr. Stamp, paragraph 12 of the statement of Mr. Crosland said that "the village of Junik was completely razed to the ground" and page 9920, line 20 and 21: "During the period of spring, Junik was systematically destroyed ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that just shows the futility of trying to sort out these matters by discussion across the courtroom. It's a matter for evidence and you can put what you consider to be an accurate reference to the witness in due course, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me, I have positive information about technical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Can we please have Defence Exhibit 1240. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just, could you stop it now, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Odalovic, are you familiar with these images?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Mr. Holbrooke's visit to the village of Junik; I think it was at the end of June 1998. This is a scene that seriously disturbed all of us because after all, this is something that we did not expect that a high-ranking diplomat would do this. On this day in the most conspicuous manner he granted full legitimacy to the so-called liberation army. If you look at the clip closely you will see that next to him is the man who calls himself Haxhija and he says he is a professor; but in any event after this the situation in Kosovo and Metohija changed entirely and it became clear who the American administration supported. You will see that Mr. Holbrooke took off his shoes, whereas everyone else is wearing shoes. This is something typical of Albanian homes, but I don't think that is relevant or important for this case. Immediately after this, Mr. Holbrooke's statement carried by Fonet further irritated us that the Serbs should leave and the Albanians should come back. Of course this can easily be found, this statement from this media company.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the second part of this clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you stop there, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, do you recognise the person shaking hands with a member of the KLA on this image?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Mr. Veton Surroi, one of the, until then, more moderate leaders of Albanians until then. He's a leader of a political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we continue the viewing of this video footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Will you stop it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, do you perhaps recognise in the top right-hand corner next to the logo of this Tribunal, which you can still see on the screen, which TV company this is?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can tell us, Mr. Cepic, and let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I hope that my assistant will play in next couple of seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To speed the procedure up -- now we can see it. In the top right-hand quarter.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the logo of the TV Shipnija or the Albanian television, and this whole gathering is obviously not something that happened by chance that -- when the national television of another state was present there filming this encounter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Odalovic ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Odalovic, my last question for you: Would the Albanian national television conceal any destruction had it existed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On what basis would he know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I withdraw my question, Your Honour, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But he has got enough experience in that region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he would need to be a student of television to tell us that, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I, as I said in the previous occasion, I had lot of material and I interviewed many people from Kosovo and Metohija and they told me almost the same sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a different matter, Mr. Cepic. Do you have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I completed my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Odalovic. I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Odalovic. My name is Branko Lukic, and I appear on behalf of Mr. Sreten Lukic in this case. I have several questions for you. First I would like to go back to your examination-in-chief when you said that the KLA crossed the Sitnica River in connection with the incident when the Belacevac mine was taken control of. Where were they in fact when they crossed the Sitnica River?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the immediate vicinity of the Kosovo thermo power-plants, that is at the entrance of the Obilic, Belacevac. They had already passed the open-cast mines from which the coal was used for the power-plants, and they had established full control over this facility and which, as I have said, caused a great deal of concern because only a few days prior to that nine miners had been kidnapped from those mines. And it may be of interest to Your Honours. They were taken off a bus. Their IDs were demanded. All of them were in one bus, both Serbs and Albanians. The Albanians were released and told not to come back to work, that the KLA was now in control, whereas the Serbs were abducted. And there were no longer be any production or work at the mines without their permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the KLA members on that occasion enter the outskirts of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Pristina itself is concerned, we had a neuralgic area called Vranjevac where they operated unhindered and most of the attacks were launched from there. As for the actual crossing of the Sitnica River and the capture of these mines. These mines are about 5 or 6 kilometres from Pristina, so very close to Kosovo Polje, but on this occasion they didn't enter Pristina without any -- with units of their own but they were present in Pristina; that is quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us when this was, if you can remember; approximately if you don't know the exact date?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the miners were kidnapped on the 22nd of June, 1998, and this was around that time because this went on for about ten days, the pressure, attacks, sabotage, and everything else that was happening at the mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were in Pristina and you know of the Hotel Grand. Did you ever see in the course of 1998 the paramilitary unit known as Arkanovci, were they ever situated there or Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, quite certainly not. The Grand Hotel was full of foreign journalists, and surely they would have noticed it. I did go to the Hotel Grand frequently but I never saw them; that's for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with the Jashari operation, were you ever consulted before the Jashari operation as to what should be done and when?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I don't see any single reason why I should be. I don't see any link between this anti-terrorist operation and myself except for the fact that two or three days after the completion of the operation I took foreign journalists and diplomats on site because tension was running high and in agreement with the officials we agreed to allow the diplomats and journalists to go there unhindered to see what was going on. So I took them there to Donji Prekaz, and representatives of MUP talked to them, explained what had happened. We saw the destruction and everything that had happened there. The media crews filmed this, their questions were answered. My role and mission in connection with that operation ended there. That is all I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you did not discuss with Sreten Lukic ever this operation or how it should be carried out?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't even remember Mr. Lukic being in Kosovo and Metohija at that time; I think he came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 headed the state security department?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. David Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who replaced him at the end of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of 1998, Mr. Gajic was replaced by Miso Vilotic, somebody I knew quite well from before, so I know that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your discussions - and we heard that you knew Mr. Vilotic well - did he ever mention that Sreten Lukic was his superior in any sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nor could it be knowing the organisation, the structures. These are two different departments that have their own separate responsibilities. So the head of the public security system, if that was Mr. Lukic's position, he couldn't be superior to the head of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have heard that you were Chief of Staff of the civil defence for Kosovo district. Can you tell me whom you were in contact with from the MUP during the state of war? Were you in contact with the SUP of Pristina or with the MUP headquarters in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My most frequent and regular contacts were with the Secretariat of Internal Affairs in Pristina and Urosevac because in the territory of the Kosovo district there were two secretariats, and the responsibilities of civil defence within the territory of the district and the whole of Kosovo and Metohija required frequently communication, contacts exchange of information with the secretariats who were operatives on the ground because the civil defence headquarters coordinated the work of municipal headquarters. And we would at our meetings give suggestions to the commanders of the municipal staffs to communicate directly with the appropriate secretariat or the OPs as they were known which were lower levels of organisation of the secretariat. So as to deal with the problem on the ground with greater ease. We didn't have high-level contacts, nor did we deal with any problems of any strategic significance. We dealt with the problems of the population and the consequences of the NATO aggression on the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in Kosovo and in Pristina during the war, did you meet any MUP generals?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to correct you. I lived in Kosovo and Metohija. I was born there, and in the war and after the war, whatever I had is down there. So of course whatever happened during the war and the NATO aggression did require meetings, not official meetings but encounters because the destruction of Pristina and everything that happened led to us meeting, but these were not any kind of formal meetings. There was no way that any -- we could give each other instructions or orders. But these were people I knew personally and it was normal for me to see them and meet with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is why I asked whether you met them, not whether you had official meetings with them. Could you tell us who of the MUP generals you met during the war, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Lukic. I think it was during the strikes on Pristina. This is a detail that illustrates the role of the civil defence. When the MUP building was hit, when we expected there to be casualties who were still alive under the ruins, and he promised to give us a machine that would lift the enormous concrete blocks. And from a building company we engaged this machine to try and clear away the rubble. And Kovac was killed on that occasion, someone from Kosovo Polje that I knew in person. So this was the kind of situation when we would meet. There may have been others, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the atmosphere among the entire population of Kosovo after the Rambouillet talks fell through, what was the prevalent mood?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us who had good intentions had hoped that the Rambouillet talks would succeed. Unfortunately, what happened caused a great deal of concern among the entire population of Kosovo and Metohija, and while the negotiations continued we were particularly concerned by continuous attacks. There were three bombs planted, two in the Kosovo district, one elsewhere at market-places and these were not selective, anyone can be a victim. The aim was to cause panic and uncertainty, and unfortunately they succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that with the beginning of the air-strikes the civilian population, primarily women, children, and the elderly, started to flee from Kosovo and Metohija. The Albanians moving towards the Macedonia and Albania and Montenegro, whereas the Serbs and other non-Albanians towards Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a fact and that is what happened. This fear and uncertainty was intensified with the first air-strikes because no one at the time knew what the aim of the NATO aggressor was. Some civilian targets were hit, and whoever had anywhere to go because Kosovo and Metohija was the most fiercely bombed, and I think in fact the first bomb fell on Kosovo and Metohija, whoever could go somewhere did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, the question that was put to you was: "Would you agree that with the beginning of the air-strikes the civilian population, primarily women, children, and the elderly, started to flee ..." Now, your answer suggests that everybody started to flee. So are you disagreeing with the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, women, children, and the civilians did leave. I saw this in Kosovo Polje, but mostly civilians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, it's plainly built into that question that the people who were leaving were women, children, and the elderly. Is that how you saw it, that the male population who were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- fighting fit remained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Most of the men remained; they sheltered their families and the men remained in their home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you account for this: Why the women, children, and elderly would leave, the men would stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were movements among the Albanian population and the Serb and non-Albanian population, but most of the men in Kosovo and Metohija of fighting age after the state of war was declared joined the regular units of the army and the police, some on a regular basis, others from the reserves, so that most of the men joined their units, took up positions. The families remained unprotected and the men felt more comfortable if they knew they had put up their families somewhere. Because it was only in Kosovo and Metohija that the war brought uncertainties. Nowhere else did that happen. In Serbia it was just a bomb, but here during the war kidnappings could take place, murders could take place, and that was the reason why most of the civilian population left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So they left because of the threat of kidnappings and murder, is that what you're saying, rather than because of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I have to intervene. In the transcript we don't that the witness said the terrorists would enter in and kill and kidnap, and that can be checked. Maybe it would confuse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. I will ask a different question in that case. Mr. Odalovic, are you saying that most Albanian men of fighting age joined the VJ or the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said that this applied to the Serbs and other non-Albanians. As for the Albanians, they boycotted the MUP and the army. That is well-known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where were the Albanian men when the children, women, and elderly were going to the borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the first part of the answer was about Serbs and other non-Albanians, what I said; as for Albanians, a large number of their men headed towards Albania, Montenegro, and Macedonia with their families. Some headed for Serbia, Bujanovac, Bresevo, Medvece, they moved towards areas populated by Albanians. These migration waves were headed in all directions and people went wherever they thought they would feel safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a suitable place to interrupt you, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, we have to have a break here. Would you go with the usher, who will show you where to wait meanwhile. We shall resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Odalovic, do you personally know whether Albanian men of military age joined the Kosovo Liberation Army of their own free will or were they drafted into the Kosovo Liberation Army in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a generally known fact when the NATO air-strikes began the Kosovo Liberation Army started spreading their propaganda to the effect that the air-strikes were meant to help them achieve their objective. It was by pure inertia that a number of other Albanians were then drawn to join the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army, but just as in 1998 they did not hesitate to recruit by force, as it were, a number of others, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say you hail from Kosovo Polje. Are you aware of the fact that in Kosovo Polje units of the so-called Arkan's men were stationed, yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in actual fact members of the SAJ unit, special anti-terrorist units, were stationed in Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite near my house in a building, a facility called Masinopromet this is a company that belongs to one of my family and neighbours. There was a unit that was stationed there and I did see them a number of times but this was not unique. There were other such buildings especially after the bombing of the MUP building that held these units. Just on the other side of my house there was a private bakery and there was a quarter-masters unit, squad, of the army. They used the facility to make bread the Albanians had left and used the building for the same purpose. Another important thing is the day after the NATO air-strikes had ended my neighbour's family had returned. They moved back into the bakery and continued to make bread. All the equipment was still there. They just picked up where they left off in a manner of speaking. They just needed to bring in more flour so they could make bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Goran Radosavljevic, nicknamed Guri?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that this man was in command of Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can rule that out all together. He was in command of a regular unit, and I can't quite remember what it was called, but I'm certain that it was just a regular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether police arrested the perpetrators of crimes, civilians and soldiers and policemen alike? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was this one meeting of the Temporary Executive Council where Mr. Lukic informed us, simply because the situation was such that we had received information to indicate that there had been cases of looting, murder, and other crimes. So we asked to get all the information to see what was going on and don't hold me to the exact figure but I think over a thousand criminal reports had been filed and over 600 persons apparently were in prisons at the time, including dozens of soldiers and dozens of policemen. I think this was sometime in May, early May, but don't hold me to it. That's as much as I know. At this meeting we requested this information and we got it; this was in relation to a variety of crimes, such as looting, killings, and everything that unfortunately a war tends to bring with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just go back slightly with you. You were asked questions about Goran Radosavljevic and you are recorded on the transcript as saying that he was in charge of a regular army unit. Did you mean to say "army unit"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's probably an error. He was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that the witness said "police," but that can be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again I think that should be checked, yes. Please continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just another area for me to cover, Mr. Odalovic. Do you know that after the arrival of KFOR in Pristina, Serbia's MUP organised for passports and personal ID documents to be issued to all citizens?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. I was to a large extent involved in organising this, in opening this office right in the middle of Pristina where my office was as well. Up until mid-2001, until I was replaced as head of district, I kept my office in Pristina. The representatives of the Ministry of the Interior who remained in Pristina issued personal documents to everyone alike, and most of those requesting were Albanians. All of this activity was being coordinated with Mr. Lukic. We had received his support at the outset and we all believed that this was something that we should be doing. Albanians believed by and large that their documents had been destroyed and torn up. We wanted to show that we and the police the same state and the same police were now providing them with personal identification papers and making it possible for them to receive what they were entitled to. That's as much as I know. Up until the time I was replaced, over 60.000 passports had been issued as well as IDs, driving licences. We even had driving tests because the international community recognised no other documents apart from the regular ones. We received confirmation the other day that over 220.000 Albanians -- because this office continues to operate. It's just that now there are problems with relocation, but over 220.000 passports were issued to Albanians by the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that because of certain problems the office was moved or relocated. Would these problems include the murder of Aco Petrovic in mid-2001 and do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aleksandar Petrovic was the head of this office, service. There was a terrorist strike in April 2001 in which he was killed. Several members of the office were wounded on the occasion. It was quite near the building in which these documents were being issued to people. It was in the centre of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt for a moment. What's the relevance of this, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness just mentioned that the whole service was displaced and that the reason why the service is displaced is because of the terrorist attacks, not because Serbia didn't want to keep this office in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I don't have any more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Odalovic. That's all from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Odalovic. You said earlier that you were appointed by Mr. Geza Farkas to be head of the armed civilian protection for your area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision on my appointment was signed by Mr. Geza Farkas, as far as I remember. It was served on me by the late Velickovic, but as far as I remember he did sign the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, is it Mr. Farkas or is it Colonel-General Farkas?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me. I wasn't directly in touch with him. Mr. Velickovic served the decision on all of us, all the heads of districts, and I suppose that all the staff commanders were appointed by the same person. Unfortunately, I don't have a copy of that decision because a part of my personal files was destroyed at the time when the building was damaged, but I think you should be able to track it down somewhere or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, but you do know that Mr. Geza Farkas was a senior member of the command of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't know which sector he was in charge of. I wasn't entirely privy so how they were organised nor, indeed, did I have any need to know about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were appointed under the Law of Defence or in accordance with the Law of Defence? I should put it that way.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So at least in a sense of appointments -- you also said -- may I move on from that. You also said you were a member of the TEC, the Temporary Executive Council in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say I was a member of the Temporary Executive Council because I wasn't. I headed a commission which was another body, the commission for humanitarian issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You attended TEC meetings, though, didn't you? I think that's what you said that you attended a meeting or meetings of the TEC?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended quite many meetings since my appointment quite regularly, and even up to that point I had sometimes been called upon to attend those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who called upon you to attend meetings of the TEC?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, meetings would be scheduled by the president of the Temporary Executive Council, Mr. Zoran Andjelkovic. Invitations would be sent out and I responded whenever I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, just one intervention the witness said: "I would always respond if I could." That's line 24 page 38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Andjelkovic, in addition to inviting you to attend these meetings, he also asked the district heads, including yourself, I take it, to assist the TEC in the work it had to do. What -- how -- in what form was the assistance or what was the nature of the assistance that you as head of a district gave to the TEC?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't give any assistance to the TEC in terms of their jobs or their functions. We would go to meetings when we were called to discuss what we were doing primarily from a humanitarian point of view. Inspections in other administrative services were attached to us. We had the most direct line of communication to the municipality president and all the issues that TEC considered paramount in its work, and we as heads of district could assist. They would call us and we could respond, but we were not part of the Temporary Executive Council, and there were no overlaps between our respective powers and jurisdictions. We were there in an official position. We would attend these meetings to inform the Temporary Executive Council on such issues as education, et cetera, that was our primary job but most of our involvement had to do with humanitarian [Realtime transcript read in error "temporary"] issues.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could both the witness's microphones be switched on. We can barely hear the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. At line 21 I believe the witness said it had to do with humanitarian issues not temporary issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So is it therefore correct to say that when Mr. Andjelkovic asked for your assistance in achieving the work of the TEC, he -- the assistance merely meant that you would attend the meetings and inform the TEC about what you were doing especially in regards to humanitarian affairs, that's what "assistance" meant?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most usually. But there's another thing that I believe is important to point out. The National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia set up the Temporary Executive Council at the proposal of the Government of the Republic of Serbia. We as a body appointed by the Government of the Republic of Serbia were responsible for helping, for making sure that the Temporary Executive Council would meet its goal, its mandate. This was a responsibility that we had; but again the Temporary Executive Council could not take any of our responsibilities away from us or put any of our responsibilities at risk for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were the head of the Kosovo district and you told us that you were responsible to the Government of Serbia. Who appointed you head of the Kosovo district?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the appointments that were made by the government. That's how it was under the constitution and all the laws that applied. It was the sole jurisdiction of the government. There would be a government meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you recalled that it was Geza Farkas who signed your appointment as head of the civil protection unit for your area. Can you recall whether it was Mr. Zoran Andjelkovic who signed the appointment as chief of the Kosovo district and can you remember that it was on the 17th of April, 1998?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the sake of precision, the district civilian protection staff did not have any units. I was not the commander of any unit. There was no command because you said a while ago that I was appointed to command a unit. That's not true. As for Zoran Andjelkovic, I'm certain about one thing. At one of its meetings the cabinet adopted the -- a decision on this appointment. As far as I remember, Zoran Andjelkovic was the president, the chairman, of the personnel commission in the government. We had regular working bodies and we had ancillary working bodies. In addition to this commission there is the personnel commission and so on and so forth and they are the ones making proposals to the cabinet at all the meetings at which all the coalition partners together exchange opinions and views and this is probably something that follows from this particular mandate that Mr. Zoran Andjelkovic held. Other than that Zoran Andjelkovic is not a person on his own who could adopt a decision on nominating a particular head. This is something that could only be done by the Government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question I asked you, sir, was a very simple question. I would be very grateful so we could move quickly if you could confine your answers to responding to the question and it was merely about who signed your appointment. Could you have a look at P978. Do you see the decision appointing you chief dated the 17th of April, 1998, it's signed by Zoran Andjelkovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see in this copy of the Official Gazette that Zoran Andjelkovic signed a decision on replacing the assistant minister of finance, but I don't see my own. I don't see it in the original. I see it in the English. Again I will say Zoran Andjelkovic. In the preamble it states that the government on such-and-such a level adopts a decision, the government adopts a decision. Zoran Andjelkovic was not there on behalf of the government, he was not prime minister or deputy prime minister, but you should ask him about this, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, can we find page 33 of the B/C/S of this exhibit? Is it on -- is it there now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's the decision appointing you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Signed by Zoran Andjelkovic in his capacity as minister of the government, correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the preamble clarifies all of this. If you read the preamble it tells you everything you need to know. I think this is entirely insubstantial. I see what you're saying but it's of no consequence. He makes appointments to various companies. This could only mean that he, as the chairman of the personnel commission… er… could have a mandate of sorts… but he could not make decisions on behalf of the government or at government meetings. His was only one vote in the cabinet as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Again, 42, 22, I believe the witness said: "Perhaps he had a mandate to sign these decisions on behalf of the government," and not "to make these decisions on behalf of the government," which is pretty important I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is very important. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You didn't attend any cabinet meetings, did you, cabinet meeting of the Government of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were meetings when as heads of districts we were invited to attend meetings, when questions related to the functioning of districts were reviewed. These were sessions devoted to particular issue and only then did I attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So there may have been a couple of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, the decision has after the signature of Andjelkovic the letters "CP" what does that stand for? Because it doesn't appear to have been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means "Svojerucno" signed by him, by himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, your appointment or the revocation of the appointment could be done by the government through the minister in the same way that you were appointed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not through the minister --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on -- no. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not through the minister. Let me repeat. This doesn't depend on the minister in person or anyone else. This is a document compiled by the government regarding appointment and revocation of appointment. All these personnel issues are discussed by a certain government body. Proposals are submitted; the commission reviews them and passes decisions. So it is only in that respect that Zoran Andjelkovic is linked to this. Also, he was one of the members of the cabinet, and there were more than ten of them. So the procedure for relief of duty is the same as for the appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Which is the same thing as what I asked you whether the revocation would be the same. Can I ask you this. Are you saying Zoran Andjelkovic would have no influence on your appointment or the revocation of your appointment? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, yes. This was a proposal that reached Zoran Andjelkovic and as president of the personnel commission he could have an opinion. Now, if he was -- his opinion was decisive and supported by the majority, then I would not have been appointed. So I assume that Zoran Andjelkovic did quite certainly support my appointment because the government was already a coalition government at the time. I apologise. You will see that the same procedure applies when the previous chief of district is being relieved of duty. So if you look up at the document first Mr. Milos Nesovic is relieved of duty and then there's the appointment of Mr. Odalovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's the document which is at 581?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 581 and 582 is the document on my appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 581 is also signed by Mr. Odalovic -- by Mr. Andjelkovic? Please forgive me.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same procedure that I've just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke -- or you said now the districts were responsible to the Government of Serbia. That means, I take it, that you could get instructions that you had to obey from the Government of Serbia in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. All instructions within the framework of our jurisdictions that were entrusted to us and we were entrusted with these duties for the territory we were covering, so we were duty-bound to implement them, such as laws, decrees, decisions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when Mr. Andjelkovic came down there as the head of the TEC, he was a member of the Government of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Andjelkovic at the time was a minister in the government, minister for youth and sport.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke -- and this is moving on now to something else. You spoke in respect to quite a few of the exhibits that you were shown by my learned friend that you were quite opposed to people organising on their own initiative or to persons who took matters in their own hands. Did you recognise any particular dangers in civilians being armed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Self organisation did not imply arming people. When I was talking about self organisation, I mentioned the example of Serbs in the surroundings of Vucitrn and Mitrovica. After their compatriots had been kidnapped, they stopped and detained 47 Albanians.
