So when I said that that was too dangerous, I was referring to this kind of taking things into their own hands, such as the law, et cetera, and that is impermissible. And that is when I insisted that state organs, state bodies, should bring their influence to bear on the kidnapped persons being released - there was several hundred of them - and that was what I meant when I was talking about self organisation and certainly not arming people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When it comes to arming people, did you recognise in your own capacity that there might well be in conditions that you have described dangers in arming civilians in Kosovo at the time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That would be dangerous because via Albania hundreds of thousands of pieces of weapons had been distributed among the Albanians. If the rest of the population were to be armed similarly, this could lead to anarchy and who knows what. So we felt that this was up to the regular troops, the regular units, and their reserves who were part of those regular forces. That was our position which we advocated. I personally in absolute terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of any programme during your tenure as chief of your district where Serb civilians were armed by the state or by state organs?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any programme nor did I take part in any such activity. I do know that reserve units were used. There was a shortage of manpower in view of the fierce terrorist activities, but I don't know of anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Serbs who detained the 47 Albanians that you spoke of, for instance, and I think you referred or that was referred to in all of the exhibits you were shown, were they armed Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, probably some of them had weapons because I assume they couldn't have detained 47 people without it. But this certainly did not have the form of kidnapping or arrest, but this was intended to exert pressure on the so-called KLA to release their compatriots. And I think this was all dealt with without any incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the last answer given by the witness, 47, line 11, the witness said that this ended up without any consequences for the Albanians, and this is not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you know if anything was done in respect to those armed Serbs who detained the 47 Albanians?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know. I didn't say that they were all armed, so I really am not familiar with the details. I said that this was a counter measure, this was a reaction, nothing more than that. I think that is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I heard what you said. You said you never heard of any programme to arm Serbs, Serb civilians. Were you aware of any programme or policy to disarm Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon the completion of anti-terrorist activities, that is in the autumn of 1998, there was - let me call it - a public campaign calling on the Albanians to hand in their weapons, to go back to their homes. And some of these activities were very successful in Metohija. As far as I can remember, several thousand pieces were handed in, because let me remind you that several hundred thousand weapons had been brought in. You see a Kalashnikov costs about 7 German marks in Albania. So a lot of weapons had come into Kosovo. That is what I know about the disarming that you asked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is all you know about disarming Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a fact that the Albanians who were called upon to hand in their weapons did not own them legally. This is a notorious fact. And all --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- disarming was carried out in the sense that they should hand in their illegally-held weapons. I don't know anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question I want to know, the programme you spoke of in the autumn of 1998, that's all you know about Kosovo Albanians being disarmed or a programme to -- for them to hand in their weapons, no other time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in these appeals guaranteeing that they would be able to return to their homes, but I know nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And apart from the appeals in the autumn of 1998 for the third time, do you know of any other time when there was a programme to relieve the Albanian civilians of arms?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of another time? I didn't understand you properly. Did you mean another time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Apart from autumn of 1998 after those operations that you spoke of, do you know of any other time when there was a policy to take away weapons from Kosovo Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any policies or any other time, so I'm afraid I can't be of any assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke of the education agreement and the three-plus-three agreement. Are you saying you referred to the education agreement as the three-plus-three agreement? Is that the same thing?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement on education or a part of that agreement and its implementation was passed on to the working group three plus three. So yes, that is part of the implementation of the agreement on education, the three plus three group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The education agreement was an agreement that was signed in 1996.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of September Mr. Rugova and Mr. Milosevic signed this agreement, and this agreement mentions three plus three. I can't remember which item it is, but it stated that the group three plus three would fully implement and technically organise the implementation of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there was another agreement that was signed on the 19th of March, 1998. Do you recall that agreement, an agreement for the purpose of implementing the 1996 agreement in terms of getting Kosovar Albanian students into schools. Do you recall in 1998 another agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it wasn't in 1996 but in 1998 -- did you say "1996"? Are you referring to 1996 or 1998, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let's go over this again. The education agreement that was signed by President Milosevic and Mr. Rugova was signed in 1996. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 1st of September, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there was another agreement later on signed in 1998, again to try to get the Kosovo Albanian students into schools. Maybe we should put it up, 1D80. Could that --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be better if I could have a look at it. I do remember, but I'd like to look at it. Quite possibly, yes. I think it was signed by the group three plus three, but I'm not quite sure. Perhaps you could show it to me. That would be a better idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 1D80, please. Are we there? If we could go to page 4 of the version in B/C/S and page 3 of the English version. It's at --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see where it's dated the 23rd of March, 1998?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who signed it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a document signed by these groups, three plus three. The Government of the Republic of Serbia appointed a group consisting of Ratomir Vico, Goran Percevic, Dobroslav Bjeletic whereas the Pristina side appointed Fehmi Agani, Abdul Ramaj, and Rexhep Osmani. And they participated in the process and as a kind of verifier on behalf of this St. Egidio community was Monsignor Vincenzo Paglia. So this was a document that was meant to implement the agreement reached. It says here that it should continue to work, that special three plus three group should be set up for all faculties and as far as I can remember there was a distribution of the premises of student hostels and other technical issues. All of this was really in implementation of the Rugova-Milosevic agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That is what paragraph 1 if you look at it indicates, that the purpose of this was to implement the Rugova agreement. I would also like you to have a look at P2885.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a question, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it there yet? Can the witness be shown the text of the letter. That's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just read the first paragraph to you, sir, because I'm not sure if there is a Serbian version. This is a letter by --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have it in Serbian? I only see it in English. Do you have a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just read the first paragraph to you, and it is a letter dated the 4th of June, 1998, from Monsignor Vincent Paglia of the St. Egidio community in which he said, and it's addressed to President Milutinovic: "At talks I had yesterday, June 3rd in Belgrade were absolutely devoid of any result because of the Serb prejudicial question which opposes to the concession of spaces of the Albanian students in the faculties inside the central campus of the University of Pristina." And he names the faculties. And he goes on to say: "The concession of spaces in that part is, however, the only way to continue the implementation of the agreement on education ..." We see from that that going almost on two years after the signing of the original education agreement and a month after the signing of another agreement to try to implement the agreement, the original education agreement, that the referees, as it were, were complaining that the Serb side was not implementing the agreement. Were you aware that the St. Egidio community was making these complaints as late as the middle of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it's not up to me to correct use -- on a previous statement that you made you called the agreement to Mr. Rugova, the Rugova agreement, but it is the Rugova-Milosevic agreement. As for this letter, I do know that Monsignor Paglia did react and that he was dissatisfied with the progress made, but it is a fact that the group three plus three until the end of March did not come to an agreement as to the implementation of the agreement. After that - I spoke about this already - once the implementation started there was certain protests and resistance, both among the teachers teaching in Serbian and others and among students, but we were determined to resolve the problem and we did in spite of resistance. There were even demonstrations. So it is quite in order, this letter, when Mr. Paglia says that it is not progressing in the way envisaged. Certain faculties that should have been provided for the Albanian students had not, and it was only to be expected that there would be problems. We were aware of the difficulty of the problem, but we also were aware that this is one of the crucial issues for future -- for a future normalisation of relations, to get the students back into schools and then we could deal with other problems. So we did have problems of that kind and this letter illustrates that, but they were overcome, quite certainly. After this we received another letter from Mr. Vico and others appointed by the government, requesting us to assist in the implementation. I think I commented on a document in Friday submitted by the Defence which shows that the entire section for building construction was being mobilised for the implementation of this document, and I was head of a board in Pristina which had to do with student hostels and I had made plans how those hostels could be distributed so that Albanian students could move in. We did some reconstruction for that purpose as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a document that speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By the time the events that were described in those documents you were shown occurred, there were many foreign observers in Kosovo and in Pristina in particular, including persons who were observing your implementation or non-implementation of the education agreement. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Monsignor Paglia also spent a great deal of time in Pristina himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So in 1996 and 1997 and before the latter part of 1998, were there -- was there any resistance to the implementation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a period of negotiations between the two three plus three groups. The greatest problem was how the groups representing Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Rugova inversely would agree on the wording itself. So this was the sort of problem they were facing, and it wasn't a small problem. The Albanians had requests and the other side had their own, so this was a problem. This is a period where a lot of responsibility rested on both sides because they had the responsibility of drawing up this implementation document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is that why there was nothing or very little implemented in that period, 1996 to 1998?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. They reached no agreement, so the question now was: What can we start implementing? The offers that were made by the Serbian side were quite clear. I really can't discuss any details because I was not a party to these talks, but I know there were a great many meetings, Mr. Vico came, Mr. Percevic, and Mr. Bjeletic. They came to Pristina several times. They would drop by my office. And then they would go to see Mr. Agani. Obviously Mr. Agani was in charge of this on behalf of Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In fact is it correct that when the technical faculty was handed over - and that is in the late autumn of 1998 - it had been destroyed and could not be used by the Albanians. So the handing over was a formality?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true there was some minor incidents, but it's not true that it could no longer be used. I believe that the Albanian representatives at the time were not prepared because I assumed they had not expected that Serbia at the time would give them over 20.000 presumably square metres of the best room, best areas, in Pristina for their new faculty. So there was some resistance by the technical faculty and by the students, but this was certainly not to the extent that it couldn't be operated right away and that they couldn't start attending lessons right away. After the Kumanovo Agreement was signed, the faculty was taken up by TMK and half of the faculty's premises still remains in their possession, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 55, line 1, after the agreement the witness said, "after the Kumanova agreement," just so we know which agreement he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Speaking of the Kumanova Agreement, if I may move on ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke about a department that you had the opportunity of working with that was involved in providing passports and other identification documents for people in Kosovo. This organisation was an organisation set up under the administration of UNMIK in Kosovo. Do you know what UNMIK is, United Nations Mission in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, UNMIK is the international mission that was set up through Resolution 1244. The service providing documents was not attached to me in terms of how it was organised. I was head of district and while working with Mr. Lukic we did everything to create the conditions for this service to begin to function. And this service -- we didn't want to do this illegally. I simply can't remember the person that Mr. Andjelkovic spoke to at the time in Pristina, but at any rate J. Carter was one of the people involved, I do remember that, and he lent his full support to the idea and to all of the activities that we pursued at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I believe the witness said the service was done in agreement with the UNMIK administration. Maybe it can be clarified by my learned colleague because the transcript doesn't show that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that a -- well, I'm not sure if the question is a translation problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's why the way to resolve it is to ask again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This service was done in agreement with the UNMIK administration; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With their knowledge and consent, that's certain. I'm not sure if there's an actual document showing that, but they certainly knew. We couldn't go on functioning without them not at all. They realised the problem was serious. Albanians had no passports, they couldn't leave the country, so the agreement was -- because I think the only documents being recognised at the time were our passports and I think this still applies. The passports are what used to be the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. UNMIK tried to start issuing some travel documents for single departures, but many countries didn't recognise those. So that was the reason why we joined the entire project.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Can we move on now to Mr. Holbrooke and what happened in mid-1998, June 1998, I think it is in June. Can we start by having a look first at 1D --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a video, Your Honours. 2D383.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "We went out looking for the people to talk to. There were roadblocks everywhere, people had put up rakes and ploughs and stuff just to block the roads. There was shooting in the area but this was clearly in Albanian control. "As the Americans hoped, the KLA were tracking them and made a kind of contact in the first village they visited. "We went upstairs in the house to sit down and we were talking to the village chief, and quite unexpectedly a rather dashing man with a beard carrying a weapon that looked larger than him came and just jammed himself in the seat. " -- And talk to us. If you want we can talk here, or we can go outside -- "There wasn't a lot of room, so he practically sat on Holbrooke's lap as if Holbrooke was Santa Claus. "In fact the Americans had got no nearer to the top KLA brass, but the KLA won valuable publicity. The picture went around the world apparently showing Americans and the KLA rubbing shoulders. "The paragraph did become part of the legend of Kosovo, and it infuriated Milosevic. "The American president got an earful" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Subsequent to -- well, before I get into that, you are familiar, I think you said, with these events. Now, you said that the meeting with the KLA person, the person was armed was staged. Were you aware that subsequent to these matters being published that Mr. Holbrooke met on several occasions with high officials of the Yugoslav state?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think right after this he was in Belgrade. I think it's in Mr. Zivadin Jovanovic's book. He explains this. He attends the conversation just after, so I suppose Mr. Milanovic [as interpreted] spoke about this, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this based on what I read in the media for the most part because I wasn't the one receiving reports from the talks in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, 58, line 6, Mr. Jovanovic, not Mr. Milanovic, spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So apart from what you were reading in the media, there was many opportunities for high state officials to clarify what the true position and the true meaning of Mr. Holbrooke's tour was, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I gave you my position, my personal view which I abide by. I suppose that other bodies spoke to Mr. Holbrooke about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this footage was done quite recently; it's not exactly contemporaneous with these events. This is post festum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see in that video when Mr. Holbrooke was touring the area that there were many buildings that were completely or almost completely demolished? Did you see that in the video just now?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the video-clip and I saw that there was a certain amount of destruction. When asked by the Defence, I did say that there had been destruction but not to the extent that was represented, that everything had been razed to the ground. Certain buildings had sustained damage but it didn't go that far. That's all I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. So the destruction that you saw in that clip just now is consistent with what you saw when you went to Junik, is it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What is shown here is just the destruction but not the buildings that remained intact. It is quite clear that this video-clip was taken just to show one side of the truth. I did see a great many buildings in a were intact, very solid. I think there is a video-clip by TV Albania and it shows a much clearer picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does he know at all where this was recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's something you can raise in re-examination -- no. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you said - but correct me if I'm wrong - that you're familiar with the footage of Mr. Holbrooke's tour that you were shown, you are familiar with the area?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the clip that was shown had been shown in the media previously. I talked about the area, I talked about when on the 16th of August I took that group of foreign diplomats and journalists there. So we passed through the place shown in the clip. That's why I know the area. It wasn't within my district just for the sake of precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, was the visit not the 16th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say the 16th of August. Maybe it was misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have heard quite a lot in this trial about the Joint Command. You say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're moving off?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm moving off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do, are you disputing the evidence of the witness that Holbrooke said that the Serbs should leave and Albanians should come back? Or is that something that's accepted?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is not accepted and that in itself is an -- it's a very vague statement as it is put by the Defence. The extent -- the meaning of it is something I would have to seek instructions because one of -- because the interpretation I put on it, and it's an open interpretation, is that he was speaking about the Serb security forces that were involved in committing atrocities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You never heard of a Joint Command and I think you said that you -- civilians in that delicate stage of Kosovo's history would not meddle in the affairs of the VJ and the MUP, civilians like yourself and Mr. Sainovic I take it would steer clear of interference in the work of these organisations. That being your evidence, sir, would it be extraordinary in your view for civilians to be participating in meetings of the MUP or of senior members of the MUP in Kosovo, including General Lukic, where they reported on the activities of the MUP? Would that be extraordinary?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a lot of different questions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give it a shot, but please warn me if I skip something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think there only is one question there, so please try to answer it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the Joint Command, I did say that in 1998 and 1999 I didn't know of it. I said in my testimony that I was there on behalf of a civilian body and our business was of a civilian nature. Due to the nature of our work, of my work, we needed to be in touch with Mr. Lukic, with the MUP, the various secretariats as lower-ranking bodies. As for anything else -- if there's anything else you would like to ask, I'd only be too happy to clarify for you. My commitment, our commitment, was for the military and police bodies to do their work. We wanted no contact between armed persons and civilians. I remember this one situation we were in a civil defence staff and some municipality people were there in uniform. We told them to take off those uniforms and put on civilian clothes because uniforms were only worn at the front line. That was our position and we stated that position in no uncertain terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As commander of the district civil defence [as interpreted] staff, I never, never put on a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As -- I'd like you to answer the question that I asked you. Your evidence being that civilians like yourself and Mr. Sainovic would steer clear of interference in the work of the MUP and the VJ, would it be extraordinary then for civilians like yourself or Mr. Sainovic to attend meetings with senior members of the MUP, like General Lukic and the heads of the SUPs where they report -- reported in detail on the work being carried out by the MUP? Would attendance at a meeting like that by civilians like yourself or Mr. Sainovic be extraordinary?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll object to the foundation of that question. If he's going to talk about a specific meeting he should provide the witness with all the details including any documents evidencing this meeting. He's asking a very specific question I think rather than a general one. If it was a general one, I think he would be okay. But he's asking a very specific question out of context that he has not formed the foundation that this witness would not have knowledge of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Stamp, that this is a general question in light of the tenure of the witness's evidence. It's an inappropriate question, and therefore that objection is repelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, I've asked the question twice now. Can you answer it, please.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're trying to make this come across as though Mr. Sainovic and I kept attending meetings together. I can't remember any such meetings. If you have a specific example, please remind me. As for my meetings with the representatives of the MUP, I told you everything about that. We received from them reports because we needed security assessments and security-related information in terms of what was going on on the ground. I suppose that's only normal if you know that we were facing an armed insurrection in 1998 and a full-scale war in 1999. It's only normal for this sort of communication to continue under the circumstances, but certainly not the way you're trying to paint it, that we were some sort of body that was there all the time and that we reported to. If you have a specific meeting to name, a specific topic that was discussed, perhaps I would love it if you could just help me and then perhaps I in turn could tell you more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, I'm going to ask you for the third time - and I'm not speaking of any specific meeting - would it be extraordinary in your view for a civilian like Mr. Sainovic to attend meetings of senior officials of the MUP in Kosovo, including General Lukic and the head of the SUPs where they reported on the activities and operations of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. The witness just said it was normal to inform the MUP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, please, this doesn't sound to me like an objection that should be being stated in the presence of the witness. Now, is there a serious point here at all? The witness has said certain things, but Mr. Stamp clearly has -- well, it's clear the answer is not entirely clear, and therefore it's open to Mr. Stamp to explore that. Reports and meetings are two different things. The witness was talking about reports, Mr. Stamp is talking about meetings, and he's entirely justified in trying to clarify the distinction between what the witness has said and what he was asking him about. So please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you do understand the question. Would --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I don't know which period you're referring to or is it a general question, but I will repeat. There was a need for us to meet. I'm -- do not know of organised meetings held on a regular basis, but I did attend meetings and sometimes I even invited members of the MUP to come to meetings at my office, but this was exclusively for the purpose of getting information about the problems occurring on the ground. And I'm deeply convinced that it is absolutely normal to have such communication in view of the situation we were in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to raise an issue now. I have a witness, Mr. Kesic, who has come from New York and he has to leave tomorrow. Mr. Odalovic is unemployed at present and he can stay here until Friday. I didn't know whether we would be meeting tomorrow - I still don't know. So could we please interrupt the cross-examination to have this other witness. I will not need more than 30 minutes, and then Mr. Stamp can continue his cross-examination later for as long as he wishes. But I'm sorry, I really, I can't organise myself in any other way. It is impossible to plan every minute in advance. Please believe me, I'm doing my very best but it's just not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, what do you say to that? The best plan might be -- can you indicate how long the cross-examination might be, just in rough terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it is going to finish today?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is definitely going to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. Fila, we'll just continue as we are and we'll face up to the problem that you pose and we will find a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I had a different idea. I thought we could hear that witness and keep this witness here and then come back to him, then there would be no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but it's going to be far better for the Bench to hear the whole of the evidence of this witness since it's only going to take another 15 or 20 minutes to complete the cross-examination. So we will adjourn now and resume at ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll resume at five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, you gave us some estimates for the numbers of missing persons who remained missing from Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, and you indicated that you are presently engaged in that area. Is the organisation responsible or charged for finding the whereabouts of persons who went missing in Kosovo and Metohija during the conflict the United Nations Office of Missing Persons and Forensic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give you an estimate. I gave you figures which are most reliable at this point in time and which have been coordinated with the International Committee of the Red Cross. As for this whole issue, this is a problem dealt with, among others, by the United Nations office that you mentioned. But Mr. Bajazet Nushi [phoen] is president of the Pristina delegation and one member is from this organisation, Mrs. Barbara -- I'm sorry, I can't remember her surname. She is a member of this Pristina delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Please, if we are going to move quickly, if you could try to confine your answers to my questions. Are you aware that the Office of Missing Persons and Forensic has its own list of missing persons from Kosovo, of whatever ethnicity, and that incorporates the ICRC figures? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably they have their own records, but I will repeat, they are incorporated in this list because we had no remarks on their part regarding our list at the working group. So I think it is absolutely in coordination with them and these figures coincide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your -- in your endeavours in this area, do you actually work with the OMPF?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On an intensive scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you're not aware of their list of missing persons? That's a simple question. You're either aware or you're not aware of their list.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of them having a different list from this one nor did they ever show it to us. I think the working group is the place where they could present it to us through their representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The list which you referred to, though, is the ICRC list?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's even a book that has been published and it is the fruit of data that we have collected, all of us together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You were asked a lot of questions and shown a lot of documents relating to humanitarian affairs in Kosovo in 1998 and what you represent to be the evidence of the Serbian authorities in that regard. You said that a directorate for regional development was set up and that provided funds and material for the reconstruction of houses that were damaged in the conflict. Do you know how many houses were rebuilt with funds from that organ?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. I told you the rough amount, about 200 million dinars were invested at the time. How many buildings, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were records kept of how many buildings were rebuilt; and if so, do you know where these records are?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were records kept, and a separate department took care of this. The directorate was in the building that Mr. Walker was housed in later on, as the verification mission. Maybe the documents can be found in the Fund For Development of the Republic of Serbia, but believe me, I can't be of greater assistance than this. But certainly records were kept on every dinar invested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You further told us that there were 11 humanitarian distribution centres for displaced persons that -- and that you were involved, you were a member of the central headquarters for all of Kosovo formed by the government in 1998. In mid-1998 I think you said there were 80 non-Albanian villages cleansed and there were 4.500 non-Albanian refugees. That is an estimate you gave to the Court as to the amount of refugees there were. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, can you recall approximately how many Kosovar Albanian IDPs that you in your planning or the humanitarian body in its planning intended to make provisions for? Simple question: What number of Kosovar Albanians you planned to make provisions for?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the Kosovo district, when we were applying for humanitarian aid, we had the figure of 112.000 persons who needed social and humanitarian aid, and on the basis of that number we made requests to the Red Cross and from the republican reserves to assist. How many people actually took this aid I don't have the records because the local headquarters, local centres for social welfare, representatives of the local self government, and of the Red Cross took care of this. But aid was envisaged for all persons who were in need at that time regardless of their ethnicity. Some centres were opened in ethnically pure Albanian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say you planned for 112.000 persons, what -- exactly what period are you talking about, if you could remember, say, the month?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the summer of the 1998 when there were movements on both sides. There were Albanians who had left their homes as well as non-Albanians. So we had envisaged aid for both, and this was the period of anti-terrorist activities so that certain inhabitants of Albanian ethnicity did move.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many displaced Albanians were there in those summer months?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was simply impossible for us to establish the exact figure, but I remember that the UNHCR - and I frequently had meetings with them - claimed that about 200.000 of them, that would be at the end of summer of 1998, August or September, the UNHCR said that about 200.000 or 220.000 people were displaced throughout Kosovo. I think they were not correct because the actions were in smaller settlements. The towns were not affected and the vast majority of the population then were living in towns, but these were their figures and I remember them well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you -- I'm not sure if you said that you -- that no records were kept. No, you said you don't have the records as to how many people received the aid, the humanitarian aid. But would you agree that in many cases the Albanian population that was displaced did not go to these centres that were set up because of a lack of confidence in the Serbian authorities by that time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question of confidence was one of the more serious problems, and we did everything to restore confidence, because the propaganda by the KLA was negative. But the Albanians did come, not in the numbers we had expected and not in all settlements. In Metohija there was less response, whereas in the central area - and I mean Podujevo, Stimlje, Urosevac, Glogovac - far more Albanians did come to pick up both humanitarian aid and also to avail themselves of the other supplies that we had provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SPS, that is the Socialist Party of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was and still am, ever since it was founded, yes, and I'm still a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. You're a member of the -- I take it because you live there, you are a member of the local Kosovo branch of the party in a leadership position there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for a leadership position in the party, it was for the first time that I was elected member of the Main Board at our congress this year; until then, I wasn't. I was president of the statutory commission and that was as far as my political positions went. Except for that, I was just a member of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look at P -- a document which we identify here as P425.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which page do you wish, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We could start from the first page, but for ease of reference we have a hard copy. I could, with the help of the usher, hand this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This, sir, is a photocopy of a book that we have of the provincial board -- or entitled: Provincial Board of the SPS of Kosovo and Metohija, proposal for means of the solution of the current problems in Kosovo and Metohija. Is that document familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago I wasn't a member of the provincial board of the SPS, but I do know that the party had certain activities, giving its suggestions, proposals, and opinions. There's no doubt about it. This document, such as it is, is one that I'm not familiar with. But if there's something specifically related to me, perhaps it would be a good idea to show it to me. I see that it was adopted on the 14th -- 15th of December, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You don't know about that document, you were not involved in the preparation of that document?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I told you, I was not a member of the board. I see certain data here. They may have collected data from the municipal boards, which are of a civilian nature. There's something I wish to comment on the first page that you may be interested in, the crime in Pec on the 14th of December, 1998, I happened to notice this. This document was passed a day after the killing of six boys in Pec --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know about that incident, Mr. Odalovic. Try to concentrate on the questions you're being asked and assist us to make progress and help the other witness arrangements. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That, Your Honours, is the cross-examination of this witness may it please you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, from my cross-examination, a cross-examination conducted by my learned friend Mr. Stamp was linked to mine, so I would like to ask the witness one more question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If something particularly prejudicial has happened, then that may be appropriate, but it wouldn't normally be appropriate for that. What is the particular problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The video-clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what is it you want to ask about the video-clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether the witness can recognise on the clip shown to him by the Prosecutor with respect to the damaged houses which location and what time is involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I asked him that and he told us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I asked him that and he told us it was in respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem is this is an exhibit that hadn't featured in the examination of the witness before Mr. Cepic cross-examined. So while it's somewhat unusual, it's I think best that we give him the opportunity to explore this. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I just say one sentence in response to Mr. Stamp's comment. I know we're in a hurry. In notifying the evidence that would be used by the Prosecutor, we didn't find evidence, a clear indication of this video-clip being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Odalovic, concerning the damage of the three or four houses, could you recognise which place is involved and when it was filmed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed that the Prosecutor showed us a clip from the period of Mr. Holbrooke's visit but I can't claim that because there are no closer indications that I could rely on, so I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I hope I'm not accused of nitpicking, but I think I should point out for the record that the clip I showed the witness was clearly indicated in our notification because it came from Mr. Fila's notification. And we indicated that anything he has put on his notification we would probably use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Odalovic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming here to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, it's just been confirmed to me that tomorrow we will be sitting in the afternoon, so that should I think overcome your problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, because this gentleman has to go back to the States tomorrow. I couldn't tell him to come on Tuesday ten days ago because I didn't know that Tapuskovic would complete his examination. I will use half of the remaining time for him and I have another witness for tomorrow. We won't be wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The name of your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next witness is Mr. Obrad Kesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Your Honour, how many questions I have for him; it's very brief. It would be a shame to send him back to the States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know from the 65 ter there's one issue I wanted to raise with you and Mr. Fila. The second paragraph of the original 65 ter says: "The witness will speak of the political reasons that led to the bombing of the FRY in the spring of'99 from the perspective of internal political relationships within the USA as well as to international standing and the role of that state in international relations." Your Honours, I'm not sure how he's going to speak as a fact witness to that not being a member of the government or any international organisation or some foreign embassy to speak to that. I'm afraid Mr. Fila is going to ask him to express his opinion as an observer. If he doesn't go into that, then I'm sure his examination will be much shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we shall see where we get to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kesic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll now be examined by Mr. Fila on behalf of Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we start, could we see 2D388.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And while waiting for it to appear on the screen could you please give us your first name and last and your occupation.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: My name is Obrad Kesic and I am currently a partner of TSM Global Consultants, which is a small company that provides advice to investors looking to invest in south-east Europe and I also work for the international foundation based in Arlington, Virginia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you also write foreign policy commentaries?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've served as a consultant and an analyst of foreign policy especially concerning south-east Europe for the US government and non-government organisations for over the last decade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please look at this photograph and explain to us in brief what it represents, who are the persons on it, and where the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: This is a meeting that was held at the White House on April 14th, 1999. The meeting was with the president of the United States, William Clinton, and there was seven representatives of the Serbian community who were present at the meeting. There were other White House staffers present, including the director of the office of public liaison and also the deputy national security advisor at the time, Mr. James Steinberg.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the subject matter discussed at the meeting? It is quite obvious that the meeting took place during the air-strikes. Another question is: who exactly said what at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: The meeting was initiated by the White House. There had been a meeting with representatives of the Albanian American community a week prior to this meeting, and my opinion is that they wanted to meet with representatives of both communities. The meeting lasted approximately about an hour, roughly. What was said is -- many things were said, so I'm not quite sure which part you would like me to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I want you to say whether any reference was made to Rambouillet and whether President Clinton said anything about those talks.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Yes. That occurred early in the discussion that we had with the president. Mr. Clinton mentioned that he quite often found himself in confrontation with members of the congress. He joked about it. He said that he likes to put himself in the shoes of others, and unfortunately does that too much with members of the US congress. At that point he went on to say that if he puts himself in the shoes of Mr. Milosevic at that time that he could see that the United States perhaps went too far with what was happening in Rambouillet, that the demand -- that the provision for allowing a referendum for the Albanians in Kosovo went too far and that he himself, if he were in the shoes of Mr. Milosevic, probably would not have signed what was presented to him in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the reasons for the air-strikes carried out against Yugoslavia at the time discussed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: There was several references to the reasons in the beginning with Mr. Steinberg. Before the president entered Mr. Steinberg presented the reasons that the United States government decided to move ahead with the bombing. These mostly pertained to what he saw to be at that time a humanitarian crisis in Kosovo, and when the president came in the president briefly referred to the intervention of NATO in those terms, but he spent most of the time talking about US policy and US interests. Specifically at some point halfway through the meeting he mentioned that the issues no longer mattered that led to the bombing, that the main issues which ensured that the bombing would continue indefinitely were that the credibility of the United States was at stake, the credibility of NATO was at stake, and his personal credibility as president of the United States was at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you hold any other meetings with people from the American administration and with President Clinton; for example, on the occasion when some American soldiers were freed who had been held captive?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had many meetings with representatives of the American government and the US administration at that time, including the secretary of state, the deputy national security advisor who was present, Mr. Steinberg, many members of the state department, various American diplomats, Mr. George Tenet the director of the Central Intelligence Agency, as well as numerous members of the US congress, both the house and the senate, and this was during -- most -- many of the meetings occurred during the period of the bombing but also over a period of years before that as well as after that. I met with the president himself on three other occasions that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was one of these meetings about those soldiers being freed in the presence of Mr. Jesse Jackson?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was the principal organiser of that trip to Belgrade for Reverend Jesse Jackson, and right after we successful returned with the three American soldiers to the United States. We had a meeting with President Clinton upon our return.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My last question. I leave the OTP five minutes more than I used up myself. My last question: Did President Clinton tell you anything when and if the delegation asked that the bombing be stopped? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Which meeting are you referring to now?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The first one -- the second one -- any meeting.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: During the initial meeting with representatives of the Serbian community in the United States, the representatives who were present of the Serbian community asked specifically for the bombing to stop as a sign of good-will, especially for the Easter holidays that were approaching. At that point the president said what I indicated in terms of why the bombing could not stop. He also indicated that if it did stop even for a short period of time it would be very difficult to get the allies within NATO to resume the bombing. And as a result, the bombing could not stop even for a very short period of time. During the other meeting with the Reverend Jesse Jackson and Congressman Ron Blagojevic who was present, the Reverend Jackson requested on the entire delegation that the bombing be stopped as a sign of good-will for the president in return for freeing the American soldiers. President Clinton more or less gave the same reasons he had given us a few weeks earlier why the bombing could not stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My last question: are you a member of the democratic party or any other party?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, the democratic party of the United States, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You probably hold US citizenship, don't you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. That's all from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any other Defence counsel wish to cross-examine? Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kesic, we didn't catch on the transcript the other company that you worked for in Virginia, can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, the International Foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: The International Foundation is associated with the national congressional prayer breakfast.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that a governmental organisation, a non-governmental --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: It's a private non-governmental organisation, an NGO, and we help and work with US congress in organising the annual national prayer breakfast that occurs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: The national prayer breakfast is an event that has been held for the last 50 years in the United States where the president of the United States is the host for the prayer breakfast itself, and over 4.000 guests are invited from the United States and internationally to come together for a morning of prayer to pray for reconciliation and peace globally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see from an internet site with particulars about yourself, we have a picture of you, but you're also listed as director of the office for governmental affairs for ICN Pharmaceuticals. Do you still hold that position?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: No, that was my previous job, previous to formation of TSM Global Consultants and also to my employment with the international organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from when did you when did you work for ICN?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: For them I worked from May 1st, 1998, to roughly May 1st, I believe, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that company associated with Milan Panic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, Milan Panic was the CEO and chairman of the board at that time of ICN Pharmaceuticals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And prior to that can you tell the Court who he was in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Milan Panic was the former prime minister of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall from when to when?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: I believe he was prime minister in the early part of going back -- I think it was 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You're also referred to as a project coordinate for IREX, I-R-E-X, can you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that should be a programme officer or maybe programme director, which was the last position I held with IREX. IREX was the international research -- and still is the international research and exchanges board and it is a non-government organisation that -- to be honest with you currently I'm not sure currently what it primarily does but when I was there we handled and managed international research exchanges with countries that were formerly communist countries; and we also administered research scholarly programmes and in my last year with IREX I ran a democratic transitions programme for countries of the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you get paid by them?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're currently paid by --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Well, there's two means in which I'm paid. First is by the international foundation and then also through my clients at TSM Global Consultants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned your involvement with Reverend Jackson, and I understand he was involved in getting some American G.I.s released and you were part of that delegation that came over in connection with that, correct.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to refer to a New York Times article or story from the 30th of April, 1999, this is page 52 in the e-court Exhibit 2918, Your Honour. This is an excerpt from that article, Mr. Kesic, it said: "Some members of the group, non-clerics, have their own agendas. One, Obrad Kesic, a Serbian American businessman said he had used his contacts in the Serbian military and government to arrange the trip and hopes to bring about an end to the allied attacks by creating disunity in Belgrade or in NATO." Had you seen that article before?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: I saw it while I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us the names of who your contacts were in the Serbian military and the government for purposes of arranging this trip? And if you need to go in private session we can do that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think there's any need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: The principal contact was a gentleman in the foreign ministry named Mr. Zoran Popovic, who has served previously in the United States and who had been my contact. He had then, upon my contacting him, contacted, I believe, the then-foreign minister, Mr. Jovanovic, and also Mr. Milutinovic. And the two of them were principal in organising the visit of the delegation by Reverend Jesse Jackson.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how about in the government, that would be your military government --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: No, no, those were the government contacts. I believe the journalist who wrote that, in addition to misquoting me also misunderstood what I was saying to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what about the part about creating disunity in Belgrade or in NATO?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: That referred to an interview on the bus [sic] that I had given to the journalist in which I said as an American citizen that I did not support the bombing and that I was hoping that the actions by Reverend Jackson would lead to an end of the bombing at least temporarily. And then given what the president had said to us in our meeting, that hopefully this would lead to a permanent end to the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you about another article. This is from -- I guess this was in connection with a television show Hardball with Chris Matthews, 16th of April, 1999, it begins at page 62 and the particular paragraph is at page 65 of e-court. The topic of that show was whether or not a peaceful solution could have been found in the Kosovo situation involving all the leaders of the world and relief organisations going to Kosovo for talks. And Mr. Matthews I guess was a host of the show and asked you: "You're from over in that part of the world, Serbia, sir, what's your reaction to this sort of a peace approach rather than a military approach? Is there anything they would respond to over there in Milosevic land short of gun-fire?" And your answer is listed as: "Well, yes. I think that's one of the tragedies of this -- is that we were told that the entire peace process had come to a halt, when in fact not all the avenues for discussion had been explored. The difference in terms of the political agreement that split the Serbs from the Albanians and from the US position was about 30 per cent to 40 per cent of the document." Are you referring to the Rambouillet document?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Finally I want to ask you about the meeting with the president. The meeting wasn't a -- the president wasn't originally scheduled to be part of that meeting as I understand it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't know he was going to be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He just popped in?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: They told us when the meeting began that he was going to join us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is from page 59 of the exhibit and this is an Associated Press article dated the 17th of April, 1999. The headline is: "President says air-strikes aimed at Milosevic not Serb people." And in paragraph 2 the article quotes the president as saying: "Our quarrel is not with Serbs in Serbia, it is not with Serbs in Kosovo, and it is not with Serbian Americans. It is with a leadership that believes it is all right to kill people and to uproot them and to destroy their family records and to erase any record of their presence in a land simply because of their ethnic heritage." Did he say that in your meeting?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Not exactly like that, but something to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And then there's a White House official quoted as saying: "The president used the occasion to convey to them what we were trying to accomplish, that our quarrel was with Milosevic and what he was doing in his campaign of ethnic cleansing." Would you agree that's what he tried to do in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Actually, he never even mentioned ethnic cleansing in the meeting which surprised us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: But he did try to explain what US policy was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you make a recording of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you take notes?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have those with you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: I don't have them with me. I have a reproduction in preparation for the testimony used to refresh my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have that with you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: It's in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we get that maybe through Mr. Fila later on?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you're quoted in this article. "Obrad Kesic, a Balkans analyst and businessman who led the delegation." And you're quoted as saying that you agreed to do everything you could to help. You were talking about working I guess or that there was a Greek delegation that was trying to get relief to Kosovo. And you mentioned that in the meeting I think you said President Clinton told you all he liked to put himself in other people's shoes and think about what it would be like in terms of their situation. You mentioned he had a meeting with an Albanian delegation, what, about a week earlier?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: About a week roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you imagine President Clinton telling the Albanians that he put himself in their shoes and he would have told them probably something different than he told you wearing their shoes; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: I could assume that he would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And he said to you that he was concerned about the bombing and that it needed to go on because he was afraid that if they didn't continue NATO would lose credibility, the US would lose credibility, and he personally as president would lose credibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: That's correct, but not in that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But this president already had a serious credibility problem by that time, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a single question, since Mr. Hannis left me three seconds. This gentleman, Milan Panic, who Mr. Kesic worked for, did he run for the position of the president of the republic against Slobodan Milosevic at the time? Was he Milosevic's opponent and by virtue of that very fact his political opponent as well?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a candidate against Milosevic for president and he also later became a leader of the opposition in Serbia and that's when I began working for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all for me, Your Honour. Again, I really need to thank Mr. Hannis for his brevity. This is becoming the established practice for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, one minor detail in the transcript at page 86, line 2, I believe it was in the question that Mr. Hannis -- I believe Mr. Hannis said that he -- that Mr. Kesic is a Balkan analyst and businessman. The analyst -- the Balkan analyst part did not appear to make it in the transcript and I just wanted to catch that before we got too far ahead of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Yours has been one of the briefer appearances here, Mr. Kesic, and I'm sure you're aware.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm grateful for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That does not make it any less important. That completes your evidence. Thank you for coming. You're now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you can help us on this. We will be sitting tomorrow afternoon from 2.15. We propose at some stage tomorrow to have the hearing that we intimated in relation to the Lukic application to bar the Prosecution from interviewing witnesses. We could have that first thing at 2.15 or we could fit it in later if that's more convenient to your list of witnesses. Can you help me on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's really simple. I will have a witness tomorrow who is the one-but-last witness in our case, and the day after we shall have three witnesses via videolink. As soon as we're done with tomorrow's witness, I believe we shall have plenty of time to deal with this problem between Mr. Lukic and Mr. Hannis. I will certainly leave more than half an hour of that time for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your estimate of the examination-in-chief of the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not over one and a half hours, and I don't think the cross should take longer than that. My learned friends from the other Defence teams might have a question or two to ask. I think a total of three or three and a half hours or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think in that event we'll allocate the first half-hour for the hearing. If it needs to overrun for good reason, then it gives us some flexibility. So that's what we'll do first and then proceed to your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I wanted to raise a question about that because this next -- Mr. Andjelkovic was noticed as being four hours for direct. I have an extensive number of exhibits and I think that estimate is ambitious and I'm concerned about the videolink witnesses being scheduled for the following day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There may have to be an interruption in Mr. Andjelkovic's evidence, but we have to get a decision out on the application that's before us so we need to deal with that first tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 28th day of August, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
